gaps.sentence: There's ___ point in complaining — no one will listen.
gaps.hint: fixed expression: ___ point in doing something
gaps.explanation: 'There's little point in doing something' means it is hardly worth doing; 'point' is uncountable here.

gaps.sentence: ___ attempts were made to contact her.
gaps.explanation: 'Several' is used with countable plurals; 'much', 'little' and 'a great deal of' need uncountables.

gaps.sentence: There are too ___ tourists in Venice in August.
gaps.explanation: 'Too many' is used before countable plurals like tourists; 'too much' is for uncountables.

gaps.sentence: She carried a suitcase in ___ hand.
gaps.explanation: 'Each hand' views the two hands individually; 'every hand' is not used for body parts this way.

gaps.sentence: One of my shoes is tighter than ___.
gaps.hint: shoes come in pairs of two
gaps.explanation: 'One ... than the other' is the pattern for two items; 'another' would suggest more than two.

gaps.sentence: Don't rush — we've got ___ of time.
gaps.hint: fixed pattern: ___ of time (no article needed)
gaps.explanation: 'Plenty of time' needs no article; 'lot of time' would need 'a', and 'much of time' needs 'the'.

gaps.sentence: ___ smells burnt in here — can you check the oven?
gaps.hint: affirmative statement about an unknown thing
gaps.explanation: 'Something' is used in affirmative sentences for an unknown thing; the request to check the oven shows the speaker believes it.

gaps.sentence: This cup is cracked — could I have ___ one?
gaps.explanation: 'Another one' means one more, unspecified; 'the other one' would mean a specific second cup.
